questions.prompt: Which comment is most worth keeping above a line of code?
choices: `# cap at 100: the API rejects larger batches`
questions.answer: `# cap at 100: the API rejects larger batches`
questions.explanation: A useful comment explains why, something the code itself cannot say; the others just restate what the code does.

questions.prompt: Match each language to how its code is run.
pairs: Compiled to machine code before it runs
Interpreted: read and executed as it goes
Compiled to bytecode that runs on a virtual machine
questions.explanation: C++ is compiled ahead of time, Python is interpreted, and Java compiles to bytecode that the JVM runs.

questions.prompt: What is the term for the specific location in a program where execution begins (for example `main` in Java and C++)?
questions.explanation: The entry point is where execution starts; Python and JavaScript use the top of the file implicitly.

questions.prompt: In Java and C++, `7 / 3` with two `int` operands evaluates to 2, not 2.333.
questions.explanation: Dividing two ints produces an int, so the decimal part is truncated.

questions.prompt: What does `17 % 5` evaluate to?
questions.explanation: `%` gives the remainder: 17 divided by 5 is 3 with remainder 2.

questions.prompt: Write `is_leap_year(year)` that returns `True` if the year is divisible by 4 and not by 100, or if it is divisible by 400; otherwise `False`.
questions.reference:
def is_leap_year(year):
    return (year % 4 == 0 and year % 100 != 0) or year % 400 == 0
questions.explanation: Combine remainder checks with and/or: (year % 4 == 0 and year % 100 != 0) or year % 400 == 0.

questions.prompt: Write `fizzbuzz(n)` that returns "FizzBuzz" if `n` is divisible by both 3 and 5, "Fizz" if divisible by 3, "Buzz" if divisible by 5, and otherwise `n` as a string.
questions.explanation: Check the combined 15 case first, then 3, then 5, and fall back to str(n).

questions.prompt: Put the parts of a three-part `for` loop in the order they run on the first pass.
questions.explanation: The initializer runs once, then the condition is checked, then the body runs, then the update.

questions.prompt: When is a `while` loop the better tool than a counting `for` loop?
choices: When you don't know in advance how many repetitions are needed
When you always know the exact repeat count
When the loop body must never run
When you need to iterate over a string only
questions.answer: When you don't know in advance how many repetitions are needed
questions.explanation: A while loop checks a condition rather than a count, so it fits cases where the repeat count depends on something that changes.

questions.prompt: What keyword does Python use to define a function?
questions.explanation: Python functions start with `def`.

questions.prompt: Which statements about scope are correct?
choices: A variable declared inside a function is local to that function
A local variable stops existing when its function finishes
A global variable is visible to every function in the file
A local variable can be read from anywhere in the file after the function runs
answers: A variable declared inside a function is local to that function
A local variable stops existing when its function finishes
A global variable is visible to every function in the file
questions.explanation: Locals exist only while the function runs, and globals are visible to every function in the file. Reassigning a global inside a function needs extra syntax, and relying on globals hides a function's dependencies.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a parameter and an argument, and why passing values through parameters is better than relying on global variables.
rubric: Says a parameter is the named placeholder in the function definition
Says an argument is the actual value passed at the call
Says globals make behavior depend on state elsewhere
Says parameters and return values make a function predictable from its inputs
questions.model: A parameter is the named placeholder listed when the function is defined, while an argument is the actual value supplied when it is called. Using parameters and return values keeps a function's behavior dependent only on its inputs, whereas globals make it depend on state scattered elsewhere in the program.
questions.explanation: A parameter is the placeholder in the definition and an argument is the actual value passed in; parameters keep a function self-contained.

questions.prompt: Write `count_vowels(s)` that returns how many characters of `s` are vowels (a, e, i, o, u), ignoring case.
questions.reference:
def count_vowels(s):
    return sum(1 for c in s.lower() if c in "aeiou")
questions.explanation: Lowercase the string and count characters found in "aeiou".

questions.prompt: Which of the four course languages does not support square-bracket indexing on strings and needs `charAt(0)` instead?
questions.explanation: Python, JavaScript and C++ all allow `name[0]`; Java uses `charAt(0)`.

questions.prompt: In Python, `"Age: " + 16` works without converting 16 to text first.
questions.explanation: Python's `+` cannot mix a string and a number; you must write `str(16)` or use an f-string.

questions.prompt: Write `sum_positive(nums)` that returns the sum of only the positive numbers in the list `nums`.
questions.explanation: Loop over the list and add only values greater than zero; an empty list gives 0.

questions.prompt: A Python list starts as `[4, 8, 15, 16]`. After `append(23)`, what does `len()` return?
questions.explanation: The list had 4 elements and appending adds one, so the length is 5.

questions.prompt: Which of these collections resize automatically by default?
questions.explanation: Python's list, JavaScript's array, C++'s std::vector and Java's ArrayList are dynamic; Java's int[] has a fixed size.

questions.prompt: What makes JavaScript's console input different from Python's `input()`, Java's `Scanner` and C++'s `getline`?
choices: It registers a callback instead of pausing to wait for input
It cannot read text at all
It reads from a file instead of the keyboard
questions.answer: It registers a callback instead of pausing to wait for input
questions.explanation: JavaScript's readline does not block; it calls a callback once the input arrives.

questions.prompt: Match each I/O term to its meaning.
pairs: Text printed after the last value
questions.explanation: `sep` and `end` shape what print writes, while stdout and stdin are the default destination and source of text.

questions.prompt: Explain why a program should never assume that text typed by a user is well-formed, and give one example.
rubric: Says user input is outside the program's control
Says it can be anything unexpected
Gives a valid example such as text where a number was expected
Says the program should check or validate it
questions.model: Input comes from outside the program's control, so the user can type anything. For example, asked for an age they might type "banana", which would crash a program that assumes a number, so the program must check the input before using it.
questions.explanation: Users can type anything, so unchecked input can crash the program or produce wrong results.

questions.prompt: In a method, what do `self` (Python) and `this` (Java, JavaScript, C++) refer to?
choices: The specific instance the method was called on
The file the class is in
questions.answer: The specific instance the method was called on
questions.explanation: They give each method access to the data of the instance it is running on.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the special method that runs automatically when a new instance of a class is created?
questions.explanation: The constructor (`__init__` in Python) sets up the new instance's data.

questions.prompt: In Python, putting a leading underscore on an attribute makes it private and stops outside code from accessing it.
questions.explanation: The underscore is only a naming convention; Python does not enforce it, unlike Java's private.
